stimulus.text: “Gatsby believed in the green light, the orgastic future that year by year recedes before us. It eluded us then, but that's no matter — tomorrow we will run faster, stretch out our arms farther. . . . And one fine morning — / So we beat on, boats against the current, borne back ceaselessly into the past.” — F. Scott Fitzgerald, The Great Gatsby (1925), Chapter 9. Verbatim excerpt, public domain.

rationales.A: Celebrating business was Bruce Barton's program, not the Lost Generation's. They scorned the New Era's values.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Hemingway, Fitzgerald, and Lewis wrote from the disillusionment of World War I, scorning business, politics, and small-town values. Some joined Stein in Paris; others wrote from New York.
rationales.C: The Lost Generation drank and mocked temperance. Support for Prohibition belonged to their critics, not to them.
rationales.D: Defending fundamentalism was Bryan's cause. The Lost Generation writers questioned tradition, they did not defend it.
rationales.general:
1. Name the group: writers Stein called the 'Lost Generation.'
2. Ask what shaped them. Background: the disorienting experience of World War I left them doubting old certainties.
3. Ask what they did with it: they scorned business, politics, and small-town values.
4. Name the shared feeling: disillusionment with mainstream American culture.
Remember: a generation's name usually comes from what it lost faith in, so ask what that was.
